# Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation — facts

> Source-anchored units about Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation: 20 across 8 sources. Each line ends in the URL and anchor it came from; `keywords:` names the lexicon terms that matched.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.4.1 · generated 2026-11-09 · 20 units · 8 sources · rights: quote -->

## Definitions

- [statement] Adaptation is not an unconditional usability improvement. Findlater and Gajos describe mixed evaluation results and usability side effects; Lavie and Meyer find that benefits depend on the task, user population and circumstances of use. (medium confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation · also: http://www.cs.tufts.edu/~jacob/250aui/AdaptiveBenefits_Lavie_IJoHCI10.pdf
- [statement] The MyUI confirmation patterns are not evidence of strict opt-in consent: the described before-adaptation dialogue proceeds if the user accepts or supplies no input before a timeout. A product requiring affirmative acceptance would need a different timeout rule. (low confidence) — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257998297_User_Control_in_Adaptive_User_Interfaces_for_Accessibility · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation

## How it works

- [statement] The W3C Working Group Note Making Content Usable advises an accessible mechanism to turn off unexpected changes and return to the previous context or settings. This is supplemental design guidance, not a requirement for WCAG conformance. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] As practitioner guidance, FuseLab recommends a nearby action that restores the previous position, plus settings to reset the layout and disable automatic arranging. W3C independently recommends an off mechanism and restoration of prior state. Treat these as design recommendations, not measured evidence that the controls improve retention or trust. (medium confidence) — https://fuselabcreative.com/the-future-of-ai-constructed-design/ · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Control or report adaptive prediction accuracy, predictability and frequency of change. Findlater and Gajos warn that these characteristics can be confounded: changing task distributions to manipulate accuracy may also change other properties of adaptation. Report the algorithm characteristics even when the experiment cannot isolate them. (low confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] An elective adaptation can preserve a stable route through the interface: Findlater and Gajos describe copying predicted items into a separate menu area instead of moving the originals. Users can use the prediction or keep using known locations; checking the prediction still imposes a cognitive cost. (low confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] In the MyUI laboratory study, participants preferred unobtrusive notification with undo when adaptations had large benefits; explicit confirmation before adaptation was more appropriate when the adaptation imposed costs. The authors recommend combining these patterns according to the expected cost and benefit rather than imposing one confirmation pattern everywhere. (low confidence) — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257998297_User_Control_in_Adaptive_User_Interfaces_for_Accessibility · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] The recent comparative menu study provides bounded evidence rather than a universal menu ranking: it used small tasks and states that its menus do not represent the whole design space. Its authors also caution that EEG findings may not generalize to other populations or tasks and call for replication with more complex menus. (low confidence) — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0164121225002675 · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] W3C’s cognitive accessibility document provides supplemental guidance rather than additional WCAG conformance requirements. Its personalization recommendations should be described as guidance, not as normative WCAG obligations. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Findlater and McGrenere distinguish three control models: adaptive interfaces let the system control change; adaptable interfaces let the user control change; mixed-initiative interfaces share control. Personalization should therefore specify who initiates and controls each change. (low confidence) — https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/edapt/papers/findlater2004.pdf · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] For disclosure and recovery, expose what changed and provide a way to reject, undo or override it. Peissner and Edlin-White define these as aspects of transparency and controllability; W3C guidance also calls for user-requested changes or an available off switch and a way back to the previous state. (medium confidence) — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257998297_User_Control_in_Adaptive_User_Interfaces_for_Accessibility · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation · also: https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/
- [statement] Evaluate efficiency and experience separately. Findlater and Gajos recommend task completion time, errors and ratings of obtrusiveness, predictability and usefulness. The comparative adaptive-menu study by Gaspar-Figueiredo and colleagues likewise distinguishes performance from preference and reports that UX and performance measures were not correlated with preference in its experiment. (medium confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation · also: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0164121225002675
- [statement] Test familiar and unfamiliar tasks and allow users to develop expertise. Findlater and Gajos explain that novice and expert users can benefit differently; in Lavie and Meyer’s driving-simulator experiments, fully adaptive behavior helped in familiar situations but increased workload and impaired performance in unfamiliar situations to which the interface had not adapted. These findings do not establish the same effects in every application. (medium confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation · also: http://www.cs.tufts.edu/~jacob/250aui/AdaptiveBenefits_Lavie_IJoHCI10.pdf
- [statement] Assess feature awareness and later task performance alongside immediate efficiency. Findlater and Gajos describe recognition tests for awareness and report that highly accurate adaptations can focus attention on a subset of features, reducing awareness of unused features and impairing performance on new tasks. (low confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] The MyUI findings have explicit limits: participants did not have the actual accessibility impairments being modeled; explanations during the experiment could bias awareness; and the study concentrated on subjective ratings. The authors call for real-world validation, objective performance data and longer-term observation without explicit explanations. (low confidence) — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257998297_User_Control_in_Adaptive_User_Interfaces_for_Accessibility · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] Keep a stable baseline in evaluations: in Findlater and McGrenere’s split-menu experiment the static menu was significantly faster than the adaptive menu; the adaptable menu was faster than adaptive only under certain conditions, and most participants preferred adaptable. These are results for the tested menus, not proof that adaptation always fails. (low confidence) — https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/edapt/papers/findlater2004.pdf · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] W3C cognitive accessibility guidance recommends user initiation or an easy way to disable changes in context, functionality and settings, plus an easy way to return to the previous state. Its pattern explicitly excepts changes essential to the activity. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] Disclose personalization options and make them easy to configure. W3C also recommends permitting rollback to a familiar interface; its route-change example explains the change and its consequences and offers approval or a one-touch return to the original route. (low confidence) — https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/ · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] Evaluate users with relevant expertise and enough exposure to learn the interface. Findlater and Gajos warn that adaptations useful to novices may hinder experts, and that motor and cognitive abilities can change the balance of benefits and costs. (low confidence) — https://kgajos.seas.harvard.edu/papers/AIMag09-AUIs.pdf · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
- [statement] A negation check also limits the claim that predictability must dominate: the Predictability and accuracy study reports improved satisfaction from both, but accuracy had a stronger effect on performance, utilization and some satisfaction ratings than predictability in its experiment. (low confidence) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1357054.1357252 · keywords: Adaptive and personalized UI user control and evaluation
